review_text_raw:
Aesthetically pleasing, good story with at the very least, decent voice acting if not great. Runs well. An interesting gameplay mechanic that has you sitting at your desk, putting together pieces of the puzzles as agents sweep the field for evidence and follow the leads you help develop. The story has you unraveling a conspiracy, using computer tools, metadata, and analyzing software to pull the narrative together. It's fascinating, and the game does a really good job at making you feel like you're truly a professional analyst, solving crimes from the comfort of a desk in Washington DC.

Problem is, the game is pretty darn short. Only about 4 hours of gameplay, and it feels deeply on rails, to the point that the puzzle portion of it feels more like a addon to the rest of the game. If you subscribe to the $1 per hour mindset, even discounted to $9, this game is technically not worth it, as the game has limited replayability. Though, the game does make up for it with the story and gameplay to a degree. It is, at the very least, a pretty impactful 4 hours, and you could get somewhat different results if you repeat the story, so there is a small sense that your choices matter. 

I might just be spoiled, coming off of The Roottrees are Dead which had a fairly similar premise of using a computer to uncover information that can fill in the blanks. But in TRaD, they introduce you to the tools and then you spend a bulk of the time using them on your own to fill in profiles on the family tree. There was a lot more blanks to fill in and time to spend fiddling around with information. With TO, you get introduced to cool mechanics and tools on your computer, and then use almost none of them ever again. The game feels like a 4 hour tutorial other than the story, which takes interesting turns and, as a flipside, keeps the player continously faced with new and interesting problems to solve. It sucks not being able to repeatedly use a mechanic I got familiar with or a handbook I just learned, but every in-game day pulls me straight in with a curveball, gameplay wise or story wise.

The ending kinda left a bad taste in my mouth. AFAIK, your choices don't really seem to affect the ending from what I saw online in guides and gameplay.

Still gonna leave it as a positive review, because I quite enjoyed this and I think the devs are absolutely cooking here. I just hope the developers consider putting more meat on the bones of TO2, because it feels like there is a ton of potential for a truly great puzzle/detective game here that only gets partially realized.

The Operator – 8/10 – A Tense and Captivating Dive into Espionage

The Operator is a stealth-driven, psychological thriller that plunges players into the shadowy world of covert operations, high-stakes intelligence, and moral ambiguity. With an engaging narrative and a compelling atmosphere, it combines tactical gameplay with deep narrative exploration, offering a gripping experience for fans of espionage games. While it may not reinvent the wheel, The Operator does a great job of delivering a tightly-paced, immersive story that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

In The Operator, you play as a field agent working for a secretive government agency, tasked with handling covert missions that blur the lines between right and wrong. The game is heavy on stealth and strategy, as you navigate through a series of complex scenarios—whether infiltrating a heavily guarded facility, gathering intelligence, or neutralizing a threat. The gameplay is tense and slow-paced, with an emphasis on thinking ahead, blending in with your surroundings, and making choices that can lead to either success or failure. It’s all about staying unseen, listening for clues, and using your limited resources wisely. The tension constantly builds as you wonder if you’ll be caught or if the consequences of your decisions will haunt you later on.

The game’s mechanics are simple but effective. You don’t have a full arsenal at your disposal like in many action-heavy titles, and that’s part of the charm. The focus here is on patience, strategy, and managing the few tools you have, whether it’s a silenced pistol or hacking equipment. The difficulty comes not from constant firefights but from the challenge of navigating through dangerous environments, avoiding detection, and managing the relationships and choices you make along the way.

One of The Operator’s strongest points is its atmosphere. The game does an excellent job of crafting a sense of isolation and tension, using sound design, lighting, and environment to its advantage. The dark, minimalist environments add to the oppressive mood, and the voice acting and soundtrack complement the sense of secrecy and paranoia that runs throughout the game. You always feel like you’re being watched, and every decision could push you deeper into the world of shadowy operatives and untrustworthy allies.

The narrative is intriguing and filled with twists, as you’ll often have to decide whether to follow orders or act according to your own moral compass. The story doesn’t just follow the usual espionage tropes—it explores themes of trust, betrayal, and the emotional toll of being part of a covert operation. The characters you meet, especially the ones you interact with the most, are well-written and add layers of complexity to the plot. The game gives you enough room to shape your own interpretation of events, but it doesn’t shy away from showing the darker consequences of a life lived in secrecy.

However, The Operator does have its shortcomings. The stealth mechanics, while solid, can feel repetitive at times, especially in the later levels where the pacing slows down significantly. There are also a few technical hiccups, like occasional AI pathfinding issues or moments when the game’s visuals don’t quite match the level of detail of the environments. Some players may also find the slower pace a bit tedious, particularly if they’re expecting a more action-packed experience.

8/10 – A Solid, Tense Espionage Experience
The Operator is a highly effective stealth game that delivers a tense, engaging experience for anyone who loves espionage narratives. While its mechanics might feel repetitive in certain sections, the atmosphere, story, and the moral complexity of the choices you make keep it captivating throughout. The game’s slow pace and emphasis on stealth give it a unique edge in a genre often dominated by faster-paced action. If you’re a fan of games that require patience and strategic thinking, The Operator will keep you hooked. It might not be perfect, but it’s a well-executed, atmospheric title that leaves a lasting impression.

review_text_raw:
If you are looking for a good puzzle/detective guy in the chair game to scratch that itch made by an indie developer to entertain you for 3 hours with great gameplay, great puzzles that don't hold your hand and are satisfying to solve, great voice acting, introducing a couple of interesting game mechanics beyond "click face and search for name here" and a pretty good linear story, then this is the game for you. I bought it at 10% off and really enjoyed it, will definitely be on the look out for the next game this developer makes, and would recommend it to anyone with the expectation that its a good indie game.  

If you are looking for a deep, multi ending detective game where choices matter and there's endless replayability, this is not the game for you. I think the two critiques I see the most of is that fact the game is short and doesn't have multiple endings. For the length side, I think complaining that a game isn't long enough is a pretty good complaint to have. The game isn't perfect, but its entertaining and I hope the developer makes a longer game in the future using the success from this game to better utilize some of the interesting game mechanics that get introduced but then not used again (there's a few). 

Whether it's worth the price is subjective. The developer gave the reasoning that it's about the length of a movie, around the price of similar games, and so that's why it's at the price that it is. I don't know how much that justifies the price for this game, which I feel is a few dollars more expensive than similar games, but since I liked the demo, the movie comparison seemed reasonable enough for me (at least given some reason instead of no reason at all) and I wanted to support the developer, so I went for it when it first released. Overall, I am very satisfied with the game, had a good time, and would buy it again. 

Not having multiple endings doesn't bother me much. If the "choices" are scattered throughout the game, I'm not replaying, solving puzzles I already know the answers too, just to change a couple of dialogue options. The same thing for if the choice is at the end and there's no individual save feature for me to go back to. I think it's fair to expect an indie developer to just make a game that's fun to play once. There's dialogue options that don't really matter, but I found the characters you interact with the most really endearing and felt connected very quickly.

review_text_raw:
If you want to feel like you're an investigator for the US government in an agency like the FBI or CIA, this game puts you there. It's more than a visual novel, but less than a full-fledged world with practically infinite choices.

Even so, it feels full and like the choices matter. Definitely some memorable moments in this. I would like a full-fledged game with many choices and outcomes, but that would deserve a higher price tag. This is what it should be for the price, and isn't too short.

The story is solid and engaging. Having worked in the government, I can say this is idealized a bit, but is definitely not ridiculous compared to crime shows. I was surprised at several points in the plot, and the way you discover the protagonist's situation and that he encounters is solid.

However, there are a few things that make it a bit realistic. It is set in the early 90s, yet the "FDI" (not FBI) have the capability to "enhance" photos like Stable Diffusion can now. There are cell phone towers and tracking, but not many people used cell phones in the US back at that time, and the ones that did had big Motorolla boxes the size of a lunch box they plugged into. They were technically mobile, but not very. The cell phone antenna had to be attached to the car roof with a magnet. And it cost over $100/mth. Sure, it wasn't uncommon for business people, and really rich people had somewhat smaller mobile phones, but still.

Also, in the boot screen, it shows a version of Linux that is "x86_64", but 64 bit didn't become really common until around 2007.

However, you can forgive these small foibles since you can consider the game as a parallel universe world; very similar, but slightly different, like how you work for the FDI instead of FBI. Perhaps in this world, they had a decade or two jump on us in technology.

I thoroughly enjoyed this and hope they put out a longer game with either more choice or perhaps getting to play more characters, or a single protagonist through a longer story arc. When it comes down to it, my only complaint with this game is that there wasn't more of it. That's a good complaint to have if it matches up with a good price, and it does. Good luck to the dev team now and in the future!

review_text_raw:
I absolutely loved The Operator. From the moment I stepped into Evan Tanner’s shoes, booting up that simulated desktop and diving into the role of a rookie operator at the Federal Department of Intelligence, I was hooked. The game didn’t just pull me into its world—it immersed me in a labyrinth of conspiracies, moral dilemmas, and surveillance, all wrapped in a retro ‘90s aesthetic with tech that felt eerily futuristic. It was nostalgic, yes, but also unsettling in the best way.

The gameplay was simple on the surface, but each task—analyzing grainy footage, cross-referencing databases, solving puzzles—made me feel like a true digital detective. It reminded me of Her Story, but stood firmly on its own legs with a tighter narrative and a mystery that grew darker and more complex with every click. The writing was spot-on, and the voice acting had a realism that drew me even deeper into the cases.

Honestly, my biggest gripe was that it ended too soon. I finished it in just a few hours, and while every minute was satisfying, I found myself wishing for more—more time in that richly constructed world, more twists, more layers. The cliffhanger at the end didn’t just tease a continuation; it practically begged for one. I’m really hoping Bureau 81 brings us a sequel that picks up right where the story left off.

Short as it was, The Operator delivered one of the most engaging and rewarding detective experiences I’ve played in ages. It made me pay attention, think critically, and trust my instincts. And I’d jump at the chance to return to that world the moment a sequel drops.

I think it's important to go into this game with the proper expectations.

This is not a "choices matter" game when it comes to narration, and the puzzle solving is also pretty minimal when it comes to interactivity. There are a few hidden things you can find but for the most part you're mainly going to be going through the motions and left-clicking your way through the story in around 3 hours.

As it is, I'd say the game is more of an interactive visual novel, and maybe a proof of concept of something that could be done using these bones as a framework for a bigger project where actions and choices have consequences down the line, and where puzzles eventually become less hand-holdy or trivial as you progress through a longer story.

This is still nice as an atmospheric story-driven game with a good ambiance that will keep you entertained for an evening, and hopefully if the game does well enough, we could eventually see a more fully-realized version of what this game appears to want to do, but can't due to its relatively small scope.

review_text_raw:
It's probably the best "PC Detective" game I've played. The puzzles make logical sense, the UI is clean, the story is mostly very good, especially in the first half, and the game doesn't hold your hand too much. The game is good at creating a tense, anxious atmosphere, and the blurry first-person scenes are also a really interesting creative choice that I enjoyed.

But it's got some pretty noticeable flaws. While most of the plot twists land successfully, the biggest reveal is very obvious by the time it arrives, and is not as shocking as the game thinks it is. The ending is rushed and unsatisfying. The VO performances range from competent to dreadful, and the script needed an editor to polish the clunky dialogue. And, most egregiously, none of your choices matter, which is always massively disappointing.

Overall, 7/10. If they make a sequel, I'll probably play it.

Great game. X-files by way of Hacknet. Sort of. 

It's very linear, there's not a ton of "choices matter" stuff here, but it the narrative is compelling, and it's got REALLY good atmosphere and vibes. 

My only real gripe with it is that the story doesn't really feel like it reaches a conclusion, more that it hit a dead end. It ties many of its loose ends up, but in a very boring way. But the journey... Whew, boy, the journey makes it totally worth it.

Took me about 2.7 hours to complete, but that's after continuing my save from the demo, the time played from which I assume did not carry over.

For $12-15 you could do much, much worse.
